## Rivers and the Dawn of Civilization

The earliest great human societies arose along river valleys. Mesopotamia, the "land between the rivers," emerged in the fertile floodplains of the Tigris and Euphrates around 3500 BCE. There, irrigation canals transformed arid land into productive fields, supporting cities like Uruk and Babylon. Similar patterns appeared elsewhere. The Indus Valley civilization flourished along the Indus River, with sophisticated cities like Mohenjo-daro featuring advanced drainage systems. In China, the Yellow River (Huang He) nurtured early Chinese dynasties, though its catastrophic floods earned it the name "China's Sorrow." The Yangtze became the economic artery of the south. These river valleys produced not only food but also the first writing systems, calendars based on flood cycles, and centralized governments capable of organizing large-scale water management.

Russian expansion followed the great river systems—the Volga, Dnieper, and Ob—allowing fur traders and settlers to cross vast distances. The river, in a real sense, taught humans to organize.
